summary: A carefully executed, unusually transparent study of what a small pilot can tell about the learning curve of a NIR/MIR ridge/PLS calibration. It offers a deterministic-equivalent identifiability bound (Proposition 1), a prior-free compatible set, a Bayesian forecaster (B-RPM), and a 38-task leakage-controlled benchmark with pre-specified hypotheses. The topic is unoccupied in recent ACA chemometrics papers. However, the proposed method does not beat the no-improvement rule on the primary RMSEP endpoint, and 4 of 5 confirmatory hypotheses failed. The main positive result is an exploratory planning case study whose framing in the highlights and cover letter overstates the numbers (72% at a requested 80% described as 'met'; savings quoted without recourse cost; one-shot B-RPM 41% success omitted). The submission also contains unfilled author and affiliation placeholders and PDF rendering defects that would trigger an immediate technical return. On substance it is borderline: it could go to review if reframed around the observability limit and compatible set, with claims tightened and length reduced.
strengths: Novel question for ACA. No 2025-2026 ACA paper forecasts calibration learning curves or uses random-matrix or deterministic-equivalent theory.

Clear conceptual result (observability horizon) that explains why power-law extrapolation is optimistic and why the no-improvement rule is hard to beat. Compatible-set coverage 91% on real data and 99% in simulation (HB4 met).

Strong design: 38 public tasks from 8 sources, group-disjoint splits, a documented leakage audit, task- and source-level statistics, Holm correction, and confirmatory and exploratory analyses separated.
Unusual honesty: failed hypotheses, a failed confirmatory replication and robustness losses are reported openly.
Practically relevant recommendations (staged second batch, random pilots, report the compatible set) and fast computation (about 0.2 s per forecast).

issues.title: Unfilled placeholders in title page, CRediT and cover letter
issues.description: The submission cannot pass Elsevier's technical check: second author name, all affiliations, corresponding e-mail, cover-letter address and date are placeholders. The manuscript would be returned before any editor reads it.
issues.evidence: Manuscript lines 3-6: '[Second author]b', '[Department, Institution, City, Country]' x2, '[e-mail]'; CRediT: '[Second author]: Validation...'; cover letter: '[Department, Institution]', '[Address]', '[E-mail]', '[Date]'.
issues.corrective_action: Fill in every author, affiliation, e-mail and date. Make the author list identical in the manuscript, the CRediT statement, the cover letter and the submission system.

issues.title: Novelty is conceptual; the proposed method does not beat the trivial baseline on the primary endpoint, and 4 of 5 confirmatory tests failed
issues.description: ACA expects a clear, quantifiable advantage over existing approaches. Here B-RPM is less accurate than the no-improvement rule (FLAT) on the RMSEP level, both within-source and cross-family. HB1, HB2 and HB3 failed, and so did the native-resolution confirmatory HC1. The positive results are (i) gain-endpoint accuracy against FLAT and RPM (but the transferred slope is better within source), (ii) prior-free compatible-set coverage (HB4, met), and (iii) an exploratory decision-calibrated planning case study on 24 tasks. Proposition 1 is a short, elementary bound inside the existing deterministic-equivalent framework, and the manuscript itself concedes that 'weak modes act as effective noise' is known [16,20]. An editor will ask whether this is a fundamental methodological development or an honest theory-plus-benchmark study better suited to CILS or J. Chemometrics.
issues.evidence: Abstract: 'pilot's own cross-validated error remained hard to beat (0.262 vs 0.282), and three of four pre-specified hypotheses failed, as did a confirmatory test'. Table 2: FLAT 0.262 vs B-RPM 0.282 and LOFO 0.292. Section 4.5: B-RPM-LOFO vs FLAT -0.030, Holm p = 0.008. Section 4.8: HC1 not confirmed. Section 4.6: Brier scores, no method beats climatology (B-RPM 0.290 vs FLAT 0.274). Section 2.4: 'That weak modes act as effective noise ... is known'.
issues.corrective_action: Without new data, lead with what is new and works: (a) the observability horizon and the compatible set as a computable diagnostic that every pilot study can report (HB4 met: 91% coverage, 99% in simulation); (b) calibrated risk-based planning. State in one sentence what is new relative to Wei et al. 2022, Hastie et al. 2022 and Canatar et al. 2021. Keep the failed hypotheses in the Results and Limitations sections, but report them in the abstract in one compact clause rather than as the central result.

issues.title: Highlight 5 and the cover letter overstate the planning result
issues.description: The data show undershooting of the requested risk, not meeting it: 72.4% delivered at a requested 80%, and 87.5% at 90%. The case study was not among the pre-specified hypotheses HB1-HB4, so it is exploratory. Cross-family calibration for the 23 soil tasks rests on a single mango task (the authors' own caveat). B-RPM also achieves this success rate by buying 2.5-3.3x the oracle size, while the slope rule buys 0.86-1.13x. The +45 pp difference is therefore a difference in risk attitude and calibration, not dominance.
issues.evidence: Highlight 5: 'B-RPM met stated planning risks with priors taken from other application families.' Cover letter: 'met the requested 80% and 90% success rates closely (72% and 88%)'. Table S2: CAL80:B-RPM-LOFO success 0.724, cost/oracle 2.525; CAL90 0.875, 3.316; CAL80:SLOPE-T-LOFO 0.278, 0.858. Section 4.7: 'for the soil tasks the cross-family calibration rests on the mango task'.
issues.corrective_action: Rewrite as, for example: 'With cross-family priors, decision-calibrated B-RPM delivered 72% and 88% success at requested 80% and 90% (transferred slope: 28% and 40%)'. Label the case study as exploratory in the abstract, highlights and Section 3.6, and report the cost alongside the success rate.

issues.title: Reference-analysis savings ignore recourse cost
issues.description: The '39% and 20% fewer reference analyses than buying Nmax' figure equals the ratio of first-round purchases (2.525/4.167 and 3.316/4.167). Table S2 also reports total cost with recourse relative to Nmax, which gives 0.770 and 0.887, i.e. savings of 23% and 11%. Failed campaigns (28% and 12%) must buy more, so the text quotes the more favourable number.
issues.evidence: Section 4.7: 'It needed 39% and 20% fewer reference analyses than buying Nmax (Fig. 9b)'. Table S2: CAL80/CAL90:B-RPM-LOFO 'total cost rel Nmax' = 0.770 and 0.887.
issues.corrective_action: Report both numbers, or define the saving with recourse as primary (23% and 11%). Do the same in Fig. 9b, or state in its caption that recourse is excluded.

issues.title: Unfavourable one-shot B-RPM result omitted from the text
issues.description: Section 4.7 reports the one-shot success and cost of the slope rule, IPL3 and FLAT, but not of B-RPM. B-RPM's point-forecast planner met the target in only 41% of campaigns, against 77% for FLAT and 70% for RPM. Staged B-RPM reached 52%. These numbers are visible in Fig. 9a and Table S2 but not discussed. Leaving them out reads as selective reporting.
issues.evidence: Table S2: ONE:B-RPM success 0.409, cost/oracle 1.357; ONE:FLAT 0.774; ONE:RPM 0.701; STG:B-RPM 0.521. Fig. 9a shows the B-RPM (point) marker at 0.41.
issues.corrective_action: Add one sentence stating that B-RPM point forecasts are mildly optimistic (41% success at 1.36x oracle). This in fact supports the authors' argument that a stated-risk rule is needed.

issues.title: Non-identifiability claim stated more broadly than proved
issues.description: Proposition 1 bounds the difference in the expected cross-validation error path under the asymptotic deterministic-equivalent approximation. The text concedes that full-data estimators (Dicker, EigenPrism) can in principle separate signal from noise, and that within a parametric family the parameters are identified in the noiseless limit. Even so, the abstract, highlights, conclusions and graphical abstract state flatly that the gain 'cannot be identified from a pilot alone' and that 'we prove' this.
issues.evidence: Highlight 3: 'The gain from more reference samples cannot be identified from a pilot alone.' Abstract: 'so the gain from more samples cannot be read from the pilot alone'. Section 2.4: 'The statement concerns the expected cross-validation path ...'; 'Estimators that use the full pilot data ... can in principle separate signal from noise'. Corollary: 'It is not an identification region in the strict sense'.
issues.corrective_action: Scope the claim everywhere to 'from the pilot's cross-validation error path (within the deterministic-equivalent approximation)' and say that full-data estimators exist but are too imprecise at p >> n0, as Section 2.4 already argues. Also replace 'generalises across materials' in the graphical abstract with 'cross-family transfer tested on soil tasks'.

issues.title: Significance claim about new applications is supported by two families
issues.description: The claim that analysts can plan 'including for new applications without previous calibrations of the same kind' rests on the case study, which contains only soils and mango (24 tasks). Non-soil cross-family transfer for level accuracy is not separately testable, because LOFO equals LOSO for those families.
issues.evidence: Abstract Significance; Section 4.7 caveats; Section 4.5: 'The test is therefore informative for the 23 soil tasks'.
issues.corrective_action: Qualify: 'in a case study with soil and fruit calibrations'.

issues.title: Theory-validation numbers in the abstract are in-sample fits and visibly biased
issues.description: The 0.130/0.153 log errors come from a 3-parameter fit to the full-pool cross-validation path, evaluated on the same task's curve. That shows descriptive adequacy, not predictive validity. Fig. 2a shows the theory curve systematically below the empirical ridge and PLS curves for KSSL-MIR:OC, ICRAF-MIR:clay and Neospectra:pH. In Fig. 2b the low-κ branches do not collapse for small n, although the text says the curves 'collapse onto a single curve'.
issues.evidence: Section 4.1; Fig. 2a (dotted theory lines below the markers in 3 of 4 panels); Fig. 2b (separated branches at κ < 1e-3 for n = 25-200).
issues.corrective_action: Describe the fit as 'fitted to the full-pool path' in the abstract. Comment on the systematic downward offset (intercept/finite-n effects) and on where the collapse fails.

issues.title: Length, density and acronym load exceed what ACA readers will accept
issues.description: About 9,500 words from Introduction to Conclusions, 41 manuscript pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, 30 supplementary tables, 52 references, and more than 20 method acronyms (B-RPM, -LOFO, -r, -0, -m10, RPM, RPM-w, RPM-T, RPM-TD, RPM-TP, IPL2/3, EXP3, LOG2, WEI, FLAT, DF-OLS, SLOPE-T, -LOFO, HB1-4, HC1, LOSO/LOFO). The design history (three stages) and the robustness sections read like an audit log.
issues.evidence: Word count of the body; Sections 3.5, 3.6, 4.8 and 4.9; Table 2.
issues.corrective_action: Cut to roughly 6,500-7,500 words and at most 7 figures. Merge Figs 3 and 4, and move Fig. 7 or Fig. 8 to the Supplementary Material. Keep about 5 comparators in the main text (B-RPM, FLAT, IPL3, SLOPE-T, RPM). Compress the design history into one paragraph and move Sections 4.8 and 4.9 to brief summaries.

issues.title: Code and pre-registration are not publicly verifiable
issues.description: The paper's credibility rests on time-stamped pre-specification and one-command reproducibility, but code is available 'on request' and the protocols are described as 'committed to the project repository', which is not public. Elsevier and ACA strongly encourage deposition.
issues.evidence: Data availability: 'will be made available on request'. Section 2.5: 'committed to the project repository'. Cover letter: 'complete code (one-command rerun) will be made available on request'.
issues.corrective_action: Deposit the code, the per-pilot outputs and the time-stamped protocol and addenda in Zenodo or OSF with a DOI, and cite it in the Data availability statement and Section 3.8.

issues.title: Rendering defects in the PDF
issues.description: An equation is missing from line 260: the calibration-size grid is blank before '(up to the pool size)'. Missing-glyph boxes appear in 'cm❑−1' (line 327 and Section 4.8) and 'H❑2O' (Section 3.1). Equations (6) and (7) carry duplicated numbers ('...|(6)  (6)').
issues.evidence: PDF page 13 line 260; page 15 line 327; Section 3.1; page 8 Eqs. (6)-(7).
issues.corrective_action: Re-typeset the equations (unicode or MathType), restore the n-grid, and check the PDF build visually.

issues.title: Broken internal cross-references and table content mismatches
issues.description: Several cross-references point to sections or tables that do not contain the cited content.
issues.evidence: (i) 'RPM-w; Section 3.6': Section 3.6 does not define RPM-w. (ii) 'in the numerical examples of Section 4.2 the difference in optimal risk is of the same order as S_T': there are no such examples in 4.2. (iii) 'freeing the alignment exponent ... most damaging choice (Section 2.4)': 2.4 is about the horizon. (iv) 'variant RPM-TD, Table 2': RPM-TD, RPM-TP, EXP3, LOG2 and B-RPM-m10 are absent from Table 2. (v) Section 4.6 cites 'our earlier analysis' with no reference. (vi) Section 4.4 points to Section 4.6 for the dominant error source.
issues.corrective_action: Fix each reference, or add the missing rows and paragraphs.

issues.title: Figure and supplementary-table numbering and citation order
issues.description: Fig. 6a is cited before Fig. 5. Fig. 6a uses pilot sizes 25/50/100/150, while the design and Fig. 6d use 25/50/100/200. Supplementary tables are not numbered in order of first citation (S14 cited first, S1 never cited). Tables S1, S10-S13, S16, S24-S26 and S30 are never cited in the main text, although S1 holds the confirmatory HB1/HB2 tests and S10 holds HB4. Table S12 prints raw floats (0.7583333333333333) and pandas headers ('400.1'), and Table S1 has word-wrapped headers ('sourc e').
issues.evidence: Section 4.3 citation order; Fig. 6 panel (a) x-axis; supplementary PDF Tables S1 and S12.
issues.corrective_action: Renumber the figures or reorder the citations. Cite every supplementary table in order. Reformat the supplementary tables to 3 decimals with proper headers. Explain the n0 = 150 choice in panel 6a.

issues.title: Reference-list formatting
issues.description: Author names are formatted inconsistently (full given names in [12]-[14], [18], [19], [24], [25]; initials elsewhere), and [27] reads 'l. E. Frank'. Several arXiv items have peer-reviewed versions: Wei et al. (ICML 2022), Bordelon et al. (ICML 2020), Jacot et al. (NeurIPS 2020), Adriaensen et al. (NeurIPS 2023), Angelopoulos et al. (ICLR 2024). Ref. [4] is an unrefereed preprint used as a key comparator.
issues.corrective_action: Apply ACA style consistently and cite the published versions.

issues.title: Abstract length and cover-letter positioning
issues.description: The structured abstract is about 280 words, above the usual Elsevier limit of 250. The cover letter calls Ali et al. 2018 (Raman classification) 'the standard answer' for multivariate calibration, which is not accurate. It also does not explain why the paper belongs in ACA rather than a chemometrics-specialist journal.
issues.corrective_action: Trim the abstract to 250 words or fewer. In the cover letter, say 'introduced to analytical chemistry by Ali et al.' and add 2-3 sentences on why ACA's readership (method developers and calibration practitioners) needs the result.

desk_decision: Technical return now, because of the placeholders and rendering defects. Once those are corrected, the substantive decision is borderline: send to review only if the claims are tightened and the paper is reframed around the observability limit and compatible set. As currently framed, desk rejection is more likely than not.
desk_reject_probability_note: 0.55 on substance after the technical issues are fixed; about 0.40 if top changes 1-5 are made. The probability of a technical return as submitted is about 1.0.

top_changes.change: Fill in every placeholder (authors, affiliations, e-mail, date, CRediT) and fix the PDF defects: missing n-grid equation at line 260, missing-glyph boxes, duplicated equation numbers, broken cross-references (RPM-w/Section 3.6, Section 4.2 examples, Section 2.4 ablation, RPM-TD in Table 2), Fig. 5/6 citation order, uncited and misformatted supplementary tables.
top_changes.why: Without this the paper is returned unread.

top_changes.change: Align every headline claim with the numbers. Highlight 5 and the cover letter should say 'delivered 72% and 88% at requested 80% and 90%', not 'met'. Label the case study as exploratory. Report its cost (2.5-3.3x oracle) and the saving with recourse (23% and 11%, not 39% and 20%). Add the one-shot B-RPM result (41%). Scope 'cannot be identified' to the CV error path within the deterministic-equivalent approximation. Qualify 'new applications' (soils plus mango only). Change 'generalises across materials' in the graphical abstract.
top_changes.why: An editor who finds one overstatement in the highlights stops trusting the rest. Accurate claims are the cheapest way to lower desk-reject risk.

top_changes.change: Reframe the contribution as a fundamental methodological result: the observability horizon plus the computable compatible set and information fraction as a reporting standard for any pilot-based sample-size claim, with B-RPM as the explicit-prior forecaster for risk-stated planning. State 3 concrete advances over Wei et al. 2022, Hastie et al. 2022 and Canatar et al. 2021. Restructure the abstract to lead with the limit and the decision rule, and keep the failed hypotheses to one clause.
top_changes.why: Answers the editor's core question about whether there is a clear methodological development, without new data.

top_changes.change: Shorten to about 7,000 words and at most 7 figures. Merge Figs 3 and 4, move Fig. 7 or 8 to the Supplementary Material, keep about 5 comparators in the main text, compress the design history, native-resolution and robustness material, and cut acronyms.
top_changes.why: The current density (41 pages, more than 20 acronyms, 30 supplementary tables) signals a specialist chemometrics or statistics paper rather than an ACA article.

top_changes.change: Deposit the code, the per-pilot outputs and the time-stamped protocols in Zenodo or OSF with a DOI, and cite it in the Data availability statement. Revise the cover letter to explain why ACA is the right venue and to drop 'standard answer since Ali et al.'.
top_changes.why: Makes the pre-registration and reproducibility claims verifiable, which is the paper's main credibility asset.

recommendation: Return for technical corrections. After correction, borderline: send to review only if claims are aligned with the numbers and the observability-limit contribution is foregrounded. Otherwise desk-reject with a suggestion to transfer to Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems or Journal of Chemometrics.
